Q: Why to specify the type again outside the class for initialization if declared in class already? A:

Why to specify the type again outside the class for initialization if declared in class already?

Because the one inside the class is only a "declaration" while the one outside the class is a "definition" and we need to specify the type when declaring/defining a variable.

then i can simply do 'i = 1;' at anywhere to define and initialize it.

No, declaration, definition and initialization are all different things in C++. Note that i = 1; is assignment while int i = 1; is definition which also includes initialization to 1. You may initialize a variable while defining it but that does not mean you don't need to specify the type. A type is required as per the rules of standard C++.

For example, we can have the following code from static documentation:

The declaration inside the class body is not a definition and may declare the member to be of incomplete type (other than void), including the type in which the member is declared:

struct S
{
   
   static S s;     // declaration, incomplete type (inside its own definition)
};

Q: How to make this stream gatherer threadsafe? A:

So I am trying to understand how thread safety works with parallel stream

For this, you should consult the API docs for the java.util.stream package, to which Gatherer belongs. Your initializer, integrator, combiner, and finisher are examples of what the docs call "behavioral parameters". The docs do not enumerate all the non-requirements for these, but they do specify two positive requirements for them, which we can only assume form a substantially complete set of requirements except where otherwise specified:

  • behavioral parameters must be non-iterfering, and
  • they must be stateless.

Both of those characteristics are defined in detail in the docs. Note in particular that the statelessness requirement applies only to the behavioral parameters themselves, so it is not violated by, for example, your integrator modifying a separate, mutable state object.

You may also want to consult the section on mutable reductions. Although the docs focus primarily on Collectors, they also apply to the intermediate result combining performed by Gatherers. The docs discuss how the whole point of combiners is to support parallel operations by combining partial results computed by different threads. We could wish that they explicitly disclaimed thread-safety requirements on combiners, but they do not. Instead, we have to rely on the already expressed requirements for behavioral parameters to be complete, but this is a natural reading of the docs, supported, among other ways, by an example involving (non-thread-safe) ArrayList.

My understanding is that since Holder class is not thread safe (the get and set methods of Holder are not synchronized), a parallel stream will not find max correctly.

Even if there were a data race, it would not be safe to assume that the result must be wrong. A data race would introduce the possibility of it being wrong, but would not foreclose the possibility of it being right. Nor even the possibility of it being consistently right in some operating environments and / or execution conditions.

Yet, it does. Is my understanding correct or is the stream framework internally synchronizes access to the state objects while performing combiner and finisher operations?

The Gatherer docs explicitly provide that

the library is free to partition the input, perform the integrations on the partitions, and then use the combiner function to combine the partial results to achieve a gathering operation.

They also provide these additional constraints on Gatherers:

Implementations of Gatherer must not capture, retain, or expose to other threads, the references to the state instance, or the downstream Gatherer.Downstream for longer than the invocation duration of the method which they are passed to.

Mention of the state instance suggests that these might be intended in part as additional constraints on the behavioral parameters of Gatherer.of(), though the docs don't actually say that. Even if so, there is still no requirement for thread safety of those parameters, much less for thread safety of the mutable state object.

Ultimately, there is no explicit documentation that the mutable state objects that Gatherers produced by Gatherer.of() deal in are free from thread-safety obligations, but neither is there any positive mention at all of any such obligations surrounding these. The latter should be taken as a moderately strong signal in itself, considering that parallel operation is expressly a consideration for streams in general and Gatherers in particular, and that the standard library's docs are quite good in general about discussing thread safety issues when they are in scope. Moreover, easy parallelism is one of the focuses of the stream API. Requiring the mutable state objects to be thread safe is exactly the kind of thing that streams do not require you to do.

Overall, yes, the stream framework -- specifically, the Gatherer implementation provided by Gatherer.of(), internally makes the provisions needed to avoid data races when gathering a parallel stream, without requiring any mutable state objects involved to be inherently thread safe. The docs don't say it in so many words, but it is true and expected.

Q: How to skip linting when particular microservices folder have changes in README? If another have code changes then it will run A:

You wrote github.second_name and github.second.pull_request.base.sha, but the contexts are github.event_name and github.event.pull_request.base.sha.

base: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' && github.event.pull_request.base.sha || 'HEAD~1' }}

Same typo is in your trigger block. on: second list and second_name should be on: and event names, though those lines are comments so they may just be paste artifacts. Drop the ref and let paths-filter default to it.

- uses: dorny/paths-filter@v3
  id: filter
  with:
    base: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' && github.event.pull_request.base.sha || '' }}

Q: A possible solution if 'hermes update' command fails A: 
C:\Users\%Username%\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m hermes_cli.main update

I found this command to be a reliable workaround! The main issue in my installation is that hermes is trying to replace the hermes.exe . But the whole update process is started with hermes.exe, so consequently it senses that the file is locked and does not allow the update to continue.

Q: Should I use AI to learn? A:

I think AI can definitely help you learn, as long as you’re not letting it do all the thinking for you. I liked what 7Swaize said about learning how to research and fact-check things yourself, because that’s probably the most important part.

I usually try to check the sources I end up reading too. For articles, I’ve found CRAAP Test useful for getting a quick idea of whether a source is actually trustworthy, looking at things like the author, how recent it is and whether the claims are backed up.

So I wouldn’t avoid AI, I’d just make sure it’s one part of how you learn, not the only one.
